extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and lawmakers interested in comparative government and jurisprudence (political philosophers, legal historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about the consequences of three forms of government (despotism, monarchy, republic) for laws, succession, property, justice, and administration. Useful for comparative analysis of institutional design and legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of the State equals conservation of the prince
rubrics_metrics.description: "La conservation de l'État n'est que la conservation du prince, ou plutôt du palais où il est enfermé.", i.e. the survival of the State depends on preserving the person/palace of the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: treaties made by a captive prince are null because a prince in captivity is 'censé être mort'; political stability focuses on protecting the sovereign's person and seat. Examples: when a prince is imprisoned a successor is placed on the throne; diplomats may treat an occupier as having replaced the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the prince is captive he is treated as dead; succession overrides treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prince is prisoner, he is presumed dead and another ascends; treaties made by the prisoner are null because the successor would not ratify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Turks negotiated separately with Peter I after being told Sweden had placed another king on the throne. Practical rule for state continuity: succession legitimacy can invalidate acts by an incapacitated sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis and end of despotism: fear and tranquility (silence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comme le principe du gouvernement despotique est la crainte, le but en est la tranquillité; mais ce n'est point une paix, c'est le silence...", i.e. despotism rests on fear and aims at enforced quiet rather than genuine peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for policy: despotisms suppress public life and commerce to avoid uprising; measures prioritize preventing agitation over citizens' freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military power vs sovereign safety in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms force is not in the State but in the army that founded it; preserving the army defends the State, yet the army is dangerous to the prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tension: institutions must reconcile state security (retain army) with personal safety of the ruler (prevent military dominance). Historical practice: diminish great military bodies or limit their autonomy to reduce threat to the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion augments authority in despotic regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion has more influence in despotisms and adds to the fear that sustains the sovereign; in Mahometan empires religion partly explains the extraordinary respect subjects have for the prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy note: intertwining religious legitimacy with sovereignty can stabilize despotism by moralizing obedience; the text cites Turkey and the Ottoman 'Grand-Seigneur' as examples where religion 'corrige' aspects of the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign ownership of land and people destroys agriculture and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prince declares himself owner of all land and heir of all subjects, cultivation and industry decline: landlords stop improving land; if prince becomes merchant all industry is ruined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard: secure private property and inheritance rights to encourage investment, cultivation and commercial activity. Anti-pattern: princely appropriation of land and successions which leads to abandonment of improvement and widespread precarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of long-term investment and improvement under despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dans ces États, on ne répare, on n'améliore rien... on ne plante point d'arbres; on tire tout de la nature, on ne lui rend rien; tout est en friche."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: absence of property security produces neglect of infrastructure and environment. Legislative implication: property law and succession rules affect long-term capital formation and public goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishing private property does not reduce greed; it intensifies corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that take away land ownership and succession do not diminish avarice; they incite greater vexations and drive elites to hoard portable wealth (gold, silver) by theft or concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation: customary limits on princely exactions (example: Ottoman practice of taking a small percentage on successions) can moderate damage; unbounded sovereign seizures produce pervasive insecurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession must be fixed and visible to prevent civil strife
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are no fundamental laws fixing succession, the crown becomes elective by the prince or his ministers, causing repeated revolutions; the best establishment is one 'qui frappe le plus les yeux' (birth and order of birth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule for constitutional design: clear, hereditary rules (e.g., primogeniture) reduce intrigue, assassinations and civil wars. Anti-pattern: arbitrary selection of successor by sovereign or ministers, which encourages fratricide and instability (examples: Turkey, Persia, Mogol, Maroc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynastic elimination and extreme precautions in arbitrary succession systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Where princes of the royal family have equal claim, successors often have their brothers strangled, blinded, or rendered mad to secure the throne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences for human costs and regime stability: arbitrary succession breeds inhuman practices and recurrent bloody vacuums; institutional safeguards should prevent such discretionary capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family weakness and abuse of marriage in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The reigning family resembles the State: extensive in appearance but reduced; princes take many wives and have so many children that genuine familial affection and loyalty decline, promoting court intrigue and the dominance of the seraglio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociopolitical effect: fragmented family ties reduce dynastic cohesion and increase palace intrigue; advises attention to familial structures in evaluating regime health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate governments require balancing powers; despotism is simple to establish
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a moderate government one must combine, regulate and temper powers (give 'a weight' to one to resist another) — a complex legislative masterpiece seldom achieved; despotism is easier because it requires only passions to establish and is uniform everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative implication: institutional design for moderation is difficult; absence of checks leads to despotism because uniform application of will is politically cheap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early majority and social effects in warm climates favor despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: In hot climates passions appear and are extinguished earlier; people marry年轻er; majority begins earlier (e.g., Turkey at 15); society requires fewer laws and formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal claim: demographic and cultural patterns (earlier adulthood) shape legal complexity and propensity toward despotism. Use cautiously — contextual observation, not prescriptive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cession of property and trust in republics versus usury in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Cession of goods is natural in republics due to trust in citizens' probity; in despotic states poverty and uncertain fortunes naturalize usury and deter large-scale commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic inference: secure property regimes and civic probity reduce interest rates and enable larger commercial enterprises; in despotisms commerce tends to be day-to-day due to high lending risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscation: useful in despotisms, destructive in republics/monarchies; should be limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Because peculation is common in despotisms, confiscations console the people and yield revenue; but in moderate governments confiscations make property insecure, harm innocent heirs, and undermine equality — Roman law limited confiscation primarily to lèse-majesté.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescription: limit confiscations to specific grave crimes (e.g., lèse-majesté) and preferably to acquired gains rather than hereditary property to preserve family continuity and equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration vs distribution of delegated power
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotism delegated power passes entire to those entrusted (the vizir is the despote himself); in monarchy the prince tempers and distributes power, retaining greater portion while delegating less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative design: monarchies benefit from partitioning authority to avoid creation of independent great men; despotism centralizes authority and forbids independent offices with enduring prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law as the will of the prince necessitates a multitude willing for him
rubrics_metrics.description: When law equals the prince's momentary will, many individuals must be willing to act as his will; officials must 'want' for him and immediately align with his desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional consequence: such systems incentivize gift-taking and rapid personal allegiance rather than rule-following; creates expectation of sudden shifts and dependence on patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of gifts as institutionalized corruption in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms it is customary to give a present before addressing a superior; even kings are not approached without a gift; princes corrupt their own favors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/legal implication: gift-exchange is normative and necessary for access; republics condemn presents as odious, monarchies rely more on honor, but despotisms institutionalize bribery as access mechanism (Plato's extreme prescription against taking presents cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards and honors: indicator of regime corruption and decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Large material rewards and extravagant honors in monarchies and republics indicate decay of principles: when honor weakens or citizenship quality declines, rulers give great rewards (examples: Caligula, Nero vs frugal good emperors like Marcus Aurelius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative criterion: abundance of extravagant rewards signals corruption; frugality in rewards is a sign of healthy civic/honour culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to accept public office: required in republics, not in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should force citizens to accept public offices in the republic (magistratures are deposits of virtue), but not in monarchies where magistracies are marks of honor and accepted at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative rule: compulsory public service sustains republican virtue; in monarchies honor-based acceptance preserves aristocratic incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting lower military rank: republican virtue vs monarchic dishonor
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen may be obliged in republics to accept a lower army post than previously held as a sacrifice to the State; in monarchies true or false honor prevents accepting degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personnel policy: republican systems can reorder ranks for civic needs; monarchies resist downward mobility due to honor culture which can undermine flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of civil and military offices by regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and military offices should be united in a republic (citizen-soldier model) and separated in a monarchy to prevent soldiers from holding civil trust and abusing force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural prescription: unify roles in republics to tie military service to citizenship; separate them in monarchies to constrain military power over civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of offices (vénalité): inappropriate in despotism, useful in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vénalité (selling offices) is bad in despotisms because the prince must be able to place and remove subjects instantly; in monarchies it creates family professions, permanence and promotes industry when advancement via wealth is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tradeoff: sale of offices can institutionalize administration and encourage investment in office-holding in monarchies, but in despotic systems it would conflict with the sovereign's need for rapid disposition of posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for moral censors in republics but not in monarchies or despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Censors are required in a republic to correct negligence, faults, dangerous examples and seeds of corruption that do not constitute crimes but undermine virtue; monarchies rely on honor and would spoil censors; despotisms do not need them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional implication: include offices that guard public morals only where civic virtue is foundational; in monarchies social honor/reproach performs some censorial role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of civil laws varies by regime: despotism simplest, monarchy most complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchies require many legal rules, tribunals and jurisprudence due to distinctions of rank and varied property categories; despotisms have little civil law because lands belong to prince and many social legal matters are handled personally by masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal design note: complexity in legislation correlates with social differentiation (fiefs, noble status) and the need to secure citizens' lives/rights; despotism flattens law but at cost of citizens' protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of criminal law: formalities as price for liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotic states justice is summary and arbitrary (e.g., pacha's simple corporal punishment), whereas in moderate governments formalities, time and expense of justice are the price citizens pay for liberty and protection of life/honor/property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial principle: procedural protections and formalities expand in republics/monarchies to secure individual rights; simplification of process reduces costs but endangers liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of textualism in judging depends on regime
rubrics_metrics.description: The closer a government is to a republic, the more judges must follow the precise letter of the law; in monarchies judges seek the spirit of the law where it is not precise; in despotisms the judge is his own rule ('le juge est lui-même sa règle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial rule: protect citizens by fixing law's text in republics; allow interpretive discretion in monarchies for flexibility; in despotisms unpredictability and personal will dominate and undermine legal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of forming judgments: deliberation in monarchies vs single-fact binary in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchic judges deliberate, exchange and reconcile opinions; republican (popular) judges present a single fact to decide (absoudre, condamner, remettre). Romans used formulas/actions to fix questions for the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural design: deliberative collegial judging suits complex cases and status distinctions; popular binary decision-making suits mass juries but requires rigid procedural framing (formulas/actions) to keep the issue clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the sovereign may be judge: acceptable in despotism, destructive in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms the prince may judge himself; in monarchies the prince must not judge because he would be simultaneously judge and party, would lose the prerogative of grace, and would destroy constitutional intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional safeguard: prohibit sovereign adjudication in monarchies to preserve separation of powers and the ability to grant mercy; historical note: Louis XIII's attempt to judge a subject was criticized as undermining monarchical constitutional role.
